arms.predicted: Pipelined bounce with channel reuse achieves server-side total_us < 900μs, read_us < 780μs (within 20% of BatchSubmit 649μs), and throughput > 2500 MB/s by eliminating per-chunk connect_client() overhead of ~544μs.
arms.observed: Throughput 2054/2022 MB/s (avg 2038 MB/s), avg latency 1.95/1.98ms. Server-side timing: read_us≈1334-1463μs (median ~1350μs), copy_us≈115-124μs (async dispatch confirmed), total_us≈1632-1746μs (median ~1650μs). Channel reuse reduced overhead vs iter-1 pipelined (read_us 1204→1350μs is marginal) but did NOT drop read_us to BatchSubmit levels (688μs). Throughput improved 16% over iter-1 pipelined (1764→2038 MB/s) but fell far short of 2500 MB/s prediction and 3054 MB/s P2P warm reference.
arms.diagnostic_note: Channel reuse alone did not eliminate per-chunk overhead. With connect_client() per chunk, read_us was 1204μs. With single channel + per-chunk ReadAsync, read_us is ~1350μs — actually slightly HIGHER than iter-1. The additional overhead per individual ReadAsync vs BatchSubmit-dispatched ops is ~21μs/chunk (1350-688=662μs/32=~20.7μs). This matches actor.rs behavior: individual ReadAsync ops use select_index(pending_ops.len()+1) for queue pair selection, while BatchSubmit pre-selects based on batch_size. The per-chunk queue selection overhead dominates. The directional improvement (16% better than iter-1 pipelined, 42% better than sequential bounce) comes primarily from cudaMemcpyAsync overlap (copy_us=119μs dispatch vs 880μs sync), not from eliminating connect_client overhead as predicted.

arms.predicted: Synchronous cudaMemcpy version shows total_us ≈ read_us + copy_us (1400-1600μs) with no overlap, proving async copies are the mechanism of h-main speedup.
arms.observed: Throughput 1969/1970 MB/s (avg 1969 MB/s), avg latency 2.03ms. Server-side timing: read_us≈1773-1948μs (median ~1870μs), copy_us≈550-588μs (median ~565μs), total_us≈1882-2052μs (median ~1960μs). The sync version is meaningfully slower than h-main async (1960μs vs 1650μs total_us), confirming async overlap provides ~300μs benefit. However, total_us is much less than read_us + copy_us (1870+565=2435μs vs 1960μs observed), indicating ~475μs of overlap even with synchronous copies due to read-ahead structure.
arms.diagnostic_note: Prediction of no overlap was wrong. Even with synchronous cudaMemcpy, the pipeline structure provides substantial overlap because the next ReadAsync is submitted BEFORE the blocking copy begins. This means the NVMe read for chunk[i+1] proceeds while the CPU is blocked copying chunk[i]. Observed overlap: 2435μs (serial) - 1960μs (pipeline) = 475μs. The read_us in sync mode (~1870μs) is significantly higher than async mode (~1350μs), suggesting that blocking copies cause the actor to process fewer completions during the read phase — possibly because the single-threaded server cannot issue new reads during blocking copy. The throughput is 1969 MB/s vs 1764 MB/s iter-1 baseline, showing channel reuse itself contributes ~12% improvement independent of async overlap.

arms.predicted: Sequential bounce produces read_us within 10% of 649μs, copy_us within 10% of 826μs, total_us within 10% of 1475μs, end-to-end latency 2.5-3.1ms.
arms.observed: Throughput 1529/1531 MB/s (avg 1530 MB/s), avg latency 2.62ms (s1), 2.61ms (s2). Server timing (single-shot samples): read_us≈687-690μs, copy_us≈880-906μs, total_us≈1580-1595μs. Read_us is within 6% of iter-1's 649μs. Copy_us is within 10% of iter-1's 826μs (actual 880-906μs = +7-10%). Total_us 1580-1595μs vs iter-1's 1475μs (+7-8%). End-to-end latency 2.62ms is within predicted range.
arms.diagnostic_note: Baseline stable. The slight throughput increase vs iter-1 (1530 vs 1440 MB/s) is within normal run-to-run variance and may reflect system warmup differences. Server-side timing phases match iter-1 within 10%.

arms.predicted: P2P warm achieves throughput within 10% of iter-1's 3082 MB/s and latency within 10% of 1.30ms.
arms.observed: Throughput 3054 MB/s, avg latency 1.31ms. This is 0.9% below iter-1's 3082 MB/s and 0.8% above iter-1's 1.30ms. Both within 1% of iter-1 values, well within the 10% criterion. Server timing: read_us=689μs, copy_us=239μs, total_us=928μs.
arms.diagnostic_note: System hardware state is stable. P2P warm performance is consistent across iterations.

discrepancy_analysis: The primary discrepancy is that channel reuse did not eliminate per-chunk overhead as predicted. The mechanism assumption was wrong: RP-2 attributed the 555μs overhead to connect_client() (13-17μs × 32 chunks). After removing connect_client() overhead with channel reuse, read_us only dropped from 1204μs (iter-1) to 1350μs (iter-2) — a marginal change and in the wrong direction relative to the 649μs BatchSubmit target. This reveals that the dominant overhead is NOT connect_client() per chunk but rather per-chunk ReadAsync dispatch overhead in the actor (queue pair selection, polling state, or channel send latency), which costs ~20μs/chunk regardless of whether connect_client() is called. The throughput improvement (1764→2038 MB/s, +16%) comes almost entirely from the async H2D copy overlap (copy_us 112μs dispatch confirmed), not from the read phase fix. The h-ablation result further clarifies: even synchronous pipelined version beats iter-1 by 12% (1764→1969 MB/s), and the async overlap adds another ~4% (1969→2038 MB/s). The pipeline structure provides substantial read-ahead even with synchronous copies.
